platforms.title: A Low Heart Rate Alert Isn't a Diagnosis by Itself
platforms.meta_description: A smartwatch flagging a low heart rate doesn't mean something is wrong by itself. Here's how bradycardia is actually diagnosed, and when a pacemaker is needed.
platforms.body_html:
A smartwatch alert flagging a low heart rate can be alarming, but the number alone doesn't tell the whole story. Whether a slow heart rate needs treatment depends on a proper diagnostic workup, not just what shows up on a wrist device.

What Counts as Bradycardia

The hearts of adults at rest usually beat between 60 and 100 times a minute. If your heart beats fewer than 60 times a minute, that's technically bradycardia — but a slow heart rate by itself isn't automatically a problem. Well-conditioned athletes commonly have resting heart rates in the 40s and 50s simply because a stronger heart pumps more blood with each beat, meaning it needs to beat less often. What actually matters clinically is whether symptoms like dizziness, fatigue, or fainting come along with the slow rate.

How It's Actually Diagnosed

The electrocardiogram (ECG or EKG) is the main test used to diagnose bradycardia, measuring the heart's electrical activity to show exactly how and when it's beating. If a standard ECG in the office doesn't capture an irregular pattern — which is common, since bradycardia can come and go — a Holter monitor may be used instead: a portable ECG device worn for a day or more that records the heart's activity through normal daily activities. For less frequent episodes, longer-term monitoring or additional tests like an echocardiogram (to check for structural heart issues) may follow. In some cases, an event monitor that can be worn for several weeks is used instead of a 24-hour Holter, specifically because it captures episodes that happen only once every few days rather than daily.

When a Pacemaker Actually Enters the Conversation

A pacemaker isn't the first response to a low number on a screen — it becomes relevant specifically if bradycardia is severe and symptomatic, meaning the slow rate is confirmed on proper testing and is causing real symptoms that affect daily function. If an underlying, reversible cause is identified first — certain medications or thyroid conditions can slow heart rate — addressing that cause comes before considering a permanent device. This is one reason a full diagnostic workup matters more than the number on a screen: a slow heart rate caused by a thyroid problem or a medication side effect can often be resolved without ever needing a device at all, once the underlying cause is identified and treated directly.

What to Actually Do With a Low Heart Rate Alert

  • Check for symptoms, not just the number on the wearable device screen — dizziness, fainting, or unusual fatigue matter far more than the raw heart rate figure.
  • Get an ECG rather than relying on wearable data alone for anything that feels off — consumer devices are a screening tool, not a diagnostic one. They're useful for noticing a pattern worth mentioning to a doctor, but not for ruling a condition in or out on their own.
  • Ask about a Holter monitor if symptoms are intermittent rather than only once — a single normal ECG doesn't rule out an occasional slow-rhythm episode.

This article is for general health information and is not a substitute for professional medical advice.
